lessons.title: 1.1 What Is a Computer?
lessons.html:
What Is a Computer?Lesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Look around you. Do you have a phone? A calculator? A game console? Believe it or not — all of these are computers. By the end of this note, you'll understand exactly why.

What Is a Computer?

In plain words

A computer is a machine that takes in information, works on it, and gives back a useful result.

Think of it like a super-smart helper that never gets tired. You give it a job to do — like solving a math problem or playing a song — and it does it, fast and without complaining!

The computer's 4 jobs

Every computer — big or small — does the same 4 basic jobs. Let's use a simple example: making juice with a blender.

JobWhat it meansBlender exampleComputer example
1. InputPutting information inYou put fruit into the blenderYou type words on a keyboard
2. ProcessingWorking on the informationThe blender chops and mixes the fruitThe computer solves a math problem
3. StorageSaving it for laterYou pour extra juice into the fridgeThe computer saves your file
4. OutputGiving you the resultYou pour out the juice to drinkThe computer shows the answer on screen

Remember it as: IN → PROCESS → STORE → OUT

Hardware is the body you can touch (screen, keyboard, CPU, memory, storage). Software is the mind that tells the body what to do (an app, a game, Microsoft Word). A computer with no software is like a body that's asleep — it can't do anything on its own!

Why this matters to you

Your smartphone takes input (you tap the screen), processes it (opens an app), stores things (your photos and messages), and gives output (shows pictures, plays sound). That means a smartphone, a tablet, a smartwatch, and even some washing machines are all types of computers!

🧪 Try it yourself: Look at 5 things around you right now: maybe a calculator, a wooden chair, a smartwatch, a rock, and a TV remote. For each one, decide: does it take input, process it, and give output? If yes, it's a computer!

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Computer

A machine that takes in, processes, and gives out information

Input

Information going IN

Output

The result coming OUT

Hardware

The physical parts you can touch

Software

The instructions/programs that run the computer

CPU

The “brain” of the computer

Study tip: You'll meet the IN → PROCESS → STORE → OUT idea again and again in this course — it's the key to understanding everything a computer does.

lessons.title: 1.2 Types of Computers
lessons.html:
Types of ComputersLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You've probably used more than one “kind” of computer today without thinking about it — maybe a phone this morning and a laptop at a cafe. Are they really the same kind of machine?

Types of Computers

In plain words

Computers come in different sizes and shapes for different jobs, but they all still do the same 4 jobs: input, process, store, output. The main difference is size, power, and what they're built for.

Think of it like vehicles: a bicycle, a car, and a truck are all “vehicles that carry you somewhere,” but you'd pick a different one depending on the job.

The main types you'll meet

TypeWhat it's likeGood for
Desktop computerA big box plus a separate screen, kept in one placeOffices, schools, heavy everyday work
LaptopA fold-up computer you can carryWorking or studying anywhere
TabletA flat touchscreen with no keyboard attachedBrowsing, reading, light work on the go
SmartphoneA pocket-sized computer that also makes callsCommunication and quick tasks anywhere
ServerA powerful computer that serves many other computers at onceRunning websites, storing shared files

Why this matters to you

Knowing the types helps you choose the right tool: you wouldn't try to write a long report on a smartphone, and you wouldn't carry a desktop computer to class. TIH's own computer lab, and the laptop or phone you may be using right now, are both real examples of these types.

🧪 Try it yourself: List every computer-type device your household owns (phone, TV with “smart” apps, laptop, game console). Sort them into desktop, laptop, tablet, smartphone, or “other.”

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Desktop

A computer built to stay in one place, usually with a separate screen

Laptop

A portable, fold-up computer

Tablet

A flat, touchscreen computer with no attached keyboard

Server

A powerful computer that provides services to other computers

Study tip: Different jobs need different types of computers — there's no single “best” one, only the best one for the task.

lessons.title: 1.3 Parts of a Computer
lessons.html:
Parts of a ComputerLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Open up (or picture opening up) a desktop computer. What do you think is actually inside that big box?

Parts of a Computer

In plain words

Every computer is built from a set of parts that each do one job, working together like a team.

Think of a computer like a school: the principal makes decisions (CPU), the library stores books (storage), the notice board holds today's information (memory/RAM), and the entrance/exit doors let people in and out (input/output devices).

The main parts, in plain English

PartWhat it does
CPU (Central Processing Unit)The “brain” — does the thinking and calculating
MotherboardThe “nervous system” — connects every part together
RAM (memory)Short-term memory used only while the computer is on
Storage (hard drive/SSD)Long-term memory — keeps files even when the power is off
Power supplyGives the computer the electricity it needs
Input/output devicesLet you put information in and get results out

Why this matters to you

When your computer feels “slow,” it's usually one of these parts struggling — often not enough RAM, or an old, full storage drive. Knowing the parts helps you understand simple problems and even talk to a technician clearly.

🧪 Try it yourself: If you have access to a desktop computer (or a picture of one opened up), try to point to and name three parts. If not, sketch a computer and label the CPU, RAM, and storage.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

CPU

The part that does the computer's thinking and calculating

Motherboard

The part that connects every other part together

RAM

Short-term memory used only while the computer is switched on

Storage

Long-term memory that keeps files even when the power is off

Study tip: You don't need to memorise every part on day one — just remember that CPU thinks, RAM remembers for now, and storage remembers forever.

lessons.title: 1.4 Computer Hardware
lessons.html:
Computer HardwareLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
If you could touch it, would you call it hardware or software? Try it on your own phone right now — touch the screen glass, then look at the WhatsApp icon. Which one is hardware?

Computer Hardware

In plain words

Hardware is every physical part of a computer that you can actually touch — the screen, the keyboard, the CPU, the wires inside.

If a computer were a human body, hardware would be the body itself: the hands, eyes, and brain — the physical parts.

Common hardware you already know

  • Monitor/screen — shows you what's happening
  • Keyboard — lets you type
  • Mouse — lets you click and point
  • CPU — the “brain” that thinks and solves problems
  • Speakers — let you hear sound
  • Printer — turns your work into paper copies

Why this matters to you

Hardware wears out, breaks, or gets old the way any physical object does — a cracked screen or a sticky key is a hardware problem, and it usually needs a real repair or replacement, not just a software fix.

🧪 Try it yourself: Walk around your home or school and list five things you can touch that are hardware. For each, say what job it does (input, output, or something else).

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Hardware

The physical parts of a computer you can touch

Monitor

The screen that shows you what's happening

Peripheral

Any hardware device connected to a computer, like a mouse or printer

Study tip: A simple test: if you can physically touch and feel it, it's hardware.

lessons.title: 1.5 Computer Software
lessons.html:
Computer SoftwareLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You can't touch WhatsApp, a game, or Microsoft Word — so what exactly are they?

Computer Software

In plain words

Software is the set of instructions that tells hardware what to do. You can't touch software, but you can see it working on the screen.

If hardware is the body, software is the mind — the thinking and instructions that make the body actually do something useful.

Two big kinds of software

KindWhat it doesExamples
System softwareRuns the computer itself, in the backgroundWindows, macOS, Android
Application software (“apps”)Helps you do a specific taskWhatsApp, YouTube, a calculator app, Microsoft Word, a game

Why this matters to you

Every time you tap an icon, open a browser tab, or send a message, you're using software. Knowing this helps you understand why “restarting” often fixes problems — it gives the software instructions a fresh, clean start.

🧪 Try it yourself: Open your phone and list five apps (software) you use most often. For each, say what job it helps you do.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Software

Instructions that tell hardware what to do

System software

Software that runs the computer itself, like an operating system

Application

Software built to help you do a specific task

Study tip: If you can't touch it but you can see it doing something on screen, it's software.

lessons.title: 1.6 Hardware vs. Software
lessons.html:
Hardware vs. SoftwareLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A friend says, “My phone is broken — it won't open any apps!” Is that definitely a hardware problem?

Hardware vs. Software

In plain words

Hardware is the physical body of a computer. Software is the mind that tells the body what to do. You need both, working together, for a computer to be useful.

A computer with hardware but no software is like a body that's asleep — it can't do anything on its own. A computer with software but no hardware doesn't exist at all — software always needs some hardware to run on.

Telling them apart

Question to askIf yes →If no →
Can I physically touch it?HardwareKeep asking
Does it appear as icons, menus, or programs on screen?Software—
Would fixing it need a screwdriver?HardwareSoftware
Would fixing it need reinstalling or updating something?SoftwareHardware

Why this matters to you

When something goes wrong with a device, figuring out “is this hardware or software?” is the very first step to fixing it — and it's exactly what a real technician does before touching anything.

🧪 Try it yourself: Think of 4 computer problems you've heard of (a cracked screen, an app that keeps crashing, a dead battery, a slow computer full of files). Label each one hardware or software.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Hardware problem

A fault in a physical part, like a cracked screen or dead battery

Software problem

A fault in the instructions/programs, like a crashing app

Study tip: When something breaks, ask “can I touch the broken part?” — it's the fastest way to sort hardware from software.

lessons.title: 1.7 Input Devices
lessons.html:
Input DevicesLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
How does information actually get INTO a computer? You're doing it right now, just by reading this on a screen you probably scrolled with something.

Input Devices

In plain words

An input device is any hardware you use to put information or commands into a computer.

Think of input devices as the computer's “senses and hands” — the way it receives what you want it to know or do.

Common input devices

DeviceWhat you use it for
KeyboardTyping letters, numbers, and commands
MousePointing, clicking, and selecting
TouchscreenTapping and swiping directly on the screen
MicrophoneRecording your voice or giving voice commands
CameraCapturing photos or video as input
ScannerTurning a paper document into a digital file

Why this matters to you

Every single thing you've ever typed, clicked, tapped, or spoken to a device started as input. Without input devices, you'd have no way to tell a computer what you want it to do.

🧪 Try it yourself: Name the input device you are using right now to read and interact with this lesson (a touchscreen? a mouse and keyboard?). Then name one input device you rarely use.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Input device

Hardware used to put information into a computer

Touchscreen

A screen you can tap or swipe to give input directly

Study tip: If it's how information gets INTO the computer, it's an input device.

lessons.title: 1.8 Output Devices
lessons.html:
Output DevicesLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
After a computer thinks about something, how does it show YOU the answer?

Output Devices

In plain words

An output device is any hardware a computer uses to give you back a result you can see, hear, or hold.

If input devices are the computer's “hands and ears,” output devices are its “voice and face” — how it talks back to you.

Common output devices

DeviceWhat it gives you
Monitor/screenShows pictures, text, and video
SpeakersLets you hear sound
PrinterTurns your digital work into paper
HeadphonesPrivate sound just for you
ProjectorShows the screen big, for a group to see

Why this matters to you

Every result you've ever seen on a screen, heard from speakers, or held as a printout came from an output device. Recognising which device is “output” helps you troubleshoot — no sound usually means a speaker or output problem, not an input one.

🧪 Try it yourself: Look around and list every output device within reach right now (screen, speakers, headphones). For each, say what kind of result it gives you.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Output device

Hardware used to give you a result from the computer

Printer

An output device that turns digital work into paper

Study tip: If it's how the computer shows YOU the result, it's an output device.

lessons.title: 1.9 Storage Devices
lessons.html:
Storage DevicesLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
When you turn your phone off and back on, your photos are still there. Where were they the whole time it was off?

Storage Devices

In plain words

A storage device is where a computer keeps files and information permanently, even after the power is turned off.

Think of storage like a notebook: you can write in it, close it, put it away for months, and when you open it again everything is still exactly as you left it.

Common storage devices

DeviceWhat it's like
Hard drive (HDD)An older-style, larger storage disk inside a computer
Solid State Drive (SSD)A newer, faster type of storage with no moving parts
USB flash driveA small, portable storage stick you can carry
Memory cardTiny storage used in phones and cameras
Cloud storageStorage kept on the internet instead of your own device (like Google Drive)

Why this matters to you

Storage is why you don't lose your photos, homework, or messages every time your battery dies. Understanding storage also explains why a device with “full storage” starts behaving strangely — there's no room left to save anything new.

🧪 Try it yourself: Check how much storage is used on your own phone or computer (Settings → Storage). Is it nearly full, or does it have plenty of room?

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Storage device

Hardware that saves files permanently, even with the power off

SSD

A fast, modern type of storage with no moving parts

Cloud storage

Storage kept on the internet instead of on your own device

Study tip: Storage is memory that lasts — it's the reason your files survive being switched off.

lessons.title: 1.10 Computer Memory: RAM and ROM
lessons.html:
Computer Memory: RAM and ROMLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Why does a computer “forget” an unsaved document if it suddenly loses power, but never forgets how to start up in the first place?

Computer Memory: RAM and ROM

In plain words

RAM (Random Access Memory) is short-term memory the computer uses only while it's switched on. ROM (Read-Only Memory) holds permanent instructions the computer needs every time it starts.

Think of RAM like a whiteboard: great for quick, temporary work, but wiped clean the moment the power goes off. ROM is more like words engraved in stone — permanent instructions that don't change or disappear.

RAM vs. ROM

RAMROM
Full nameRandom Access MemoryRead-Only Memory
Lasts when powered off?No — wiped cleanYes — stays permanently
Used forPrograms currently runningBasic startup instructions
Can you change it?Yes, constantly, while workingRarely, if ever

Why this matters to you

This is exactly why an unsaved document disappears if the power cuts out (it was only in RAM), but your computer still knows how to switch on every single time (that part is in ROM). Saving your work moves it from temporary RAM into permanent storage.

🧪 Try it yourself: Next time you're working on a document, notice the “Save” button. Explain in your own words why clicking Save matters, using the words RAM and storage.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

RAM

Short-term memory used only while the computer is switched on

ROM

Permanent memory holding the instructions a computer needs to start up

Study tip: RAM is temporary and fast; ROM and storage are permanent. Always save your work before RAM gets wiped!

lessons.title: 2.1 Starting and Shutting Down a Computer
lessons.html:
Starting and Shutting Down a ComputerLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You press a button and, seconds later, your whole screen lights up. What is actually happening in between?

Starting and Shutting Down a Computer

In plain words

Starting up (booting) is the process a computer goes through to wake up and get ready to use. Shutting down is the safe process of turning it off properly.

Think of starting up like a person waking up: stretching, checking the day's plan, then getting ready to work — it takes a few moments, not zero.

Doing it the right way

ActionHow to do itWhy it matters
Start upPress the power button once and waitGives the computer time to load everything it needs
Shut downUse the Start Menu → Power → Shut downLets the computer save and close everything safely
RestartUse the Start Menu → Power → RestartClears small problems by starting fresh
SleepClose the lid or choose SleepPauses quickly without fully shutting down

Why this matters to you

Simply holding the power button to force a shutdown, or pulling the plug, skips the safe saving process — this is one of the most common ways people accidentally lose unsaved work or damage files.

🧪 Try it yourself: Next time you finish using a computer, shut it down the proper way through the Start Menu instead of just closing the screen, and notice how it takes a moment to close everything first.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Boot up

The process of a computer starting and getting ready to use

Shut down

Safely turning a computer off through its menu, not by force

Restart

Shutting down and starting up again immediately

Study tip: Always give a computer a proper, gentle shutdown — it protects your files and the machine itself.

lessons.title: 2.2 Using the Keyboard
lessons.html:
Using the KeyboardLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
How many different keys do you think are on a standard keyboard — and does every single one just type a letter?

Using the Keyboard

In plain words

The keyboard is the main input device you use to type letters, numbers, and commands into a computer.

Think of the keyboard like a piano: most keys make a simple “note” (a letter), but a few special keys change what the other keys do, the way a piano's pedals change the sound.

Key groups you'll use every day

Key groupExamplesWhat it does
Letter/number keysA–Z, 0–9Types the actual character shown
Enter↵Confirms an action or starts a new line
Shift⇧Types a capital letter or the upper symbol on a key
Backspace/Delete⌫Removes text before/after the cursor
Arrow keys↑ ↓ ← →Moves the cursor around the screen
Spacebar(long bottom bar)Adds a space between words

Why this matters to you

Learning to type accurately and comfortably is one of the most useful everyday computer skills — it's used in nearly every lesson in this course, from writing an email to building a spreadsheet.

🧪 Try it yourself: Open any text box (like a Notes app) and type your full name using Shift to correctly capitalise the first letters, then use Backspace to fix one deliberate mistake.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Keyboard shortcut

A key combination that performs an action quickly, like Ctrl+C to copy

Cursor

The blinking line that shows where your next typed letter will appear

Shift key

A key that types capital letters or upper symbols when held down

Study tip: Practising typing a little every day builds speed and accuracy far faster than typing occasionally in long bursts.

lessons.title: 2.3 Using a Computer Mouse
lessons.html:
Using a Computer MouseLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Have you ever double-clicked something by accident, or clicked the wrong button, and wondered why the computer reacted strangely?

Using a Computer Mouse

In plain words

A mouse is an input device you move across a surface to point at, select, and interact with things on screen.

Think of the mouse pointer as your finger pointing at things in the real world — except this “finger” can click, drag, and scroll too.

The main mouse actions

ActionHow to do itWhat it does
Click (left)Press the left button onceSelects or opens something
Double-clickPress the left button twice, quicklyOpens a file or program
Right-clickPress the right button onceShows a menu of extra options
DragHold the left button and move the mouseMoves an item from one place to another
ScrollRoll the wheel between the buttonsMoves up or down a page

Why this matters to you

Almost every action in this course — opening a file, formatting text, clicking a button — starts with the mouse. Mixing up a single click and a double-click is the single most common early mistake, and it's completely normal at first.

🧪 Try it yourself: Open any folder on a computer. Practise: single-click a file (notice it just gets selected), then double-click it (notice it opens), then right-click it (notice a menu appears).

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Click

Pressing the left mouse button once to select or open something

Double-click

Clicking the left button twice quickly to open a file or program

Right-click

Clicking the right button to open a menu of extra options

Study tip: When in doubt: single-click to select, double-click to open, right-click to see your options.

lessons.title: 2.4 Understanding the Desktop
lessons.html:
Understanding the DesktopLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
The very first screen you see after starting a computer — have you ever wondered why it's called a “desktop” at all?

Understanding the Desktop

In plain words

The desktop is the main screen of a computer, shown after startup, where you see icons, a background picture, and the taskbar.

It's called a “desktop” because it works like a real desk: you spread out files (icons) and tools (shortcuts) on it so they're easy to reach.

What's actually on the desktop

ElementWhat it is
IconsSmall pictures representing files, folders, or programs
WallpaperThe background picture or colour
TaskbarThe bar (usually at the bottom) showing open programs and the clock
Start Menu buttonOpens the main menu to find programs and settings

Why this matters to you

The desktop is your “home base” — nearly every task starts or ends here. Knowing how to organise it (rather than leaving hundreds of icons scattered everywhere) makes finding your files much faster.

🧪 Try it yourself: Look at your own (or a lab) computer's desktop. Count how many icons are on it, and identify the taskbar and Start Menu button.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Desktop

The main screen shown after a computer starts up

Icon

A small picture representing a file, folder, or program

Wallpaper

The background picture or colour of the desktop

Study tip: A tidy desktop with only the icons you actually use makes every other lesson in this course easier.

lessons.html:
Using Windows IconsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Why does a folder icon look like a folder, and a trash-bin icon look like a bin? Is that just decoration?

Using Windows Icons

In plain words

An icon is a small picture that represents a file, folder, program, or shortcut, so you can recognise and open it at a glance.

Icons are like road signs: a picture of a folder tells you “this holds files” before you even open it, the same way a picture of a fork and knife tells you “restaurant ahead.”

Common icon types

Icon looks likeWhat it usually means
A folder shapeA folder holding other files or folders
A page with a corner foldedA single document or file
A small arrow in the cornerA shortcut, pointing to the real file elsewhere
A trash binThe Recycle Bin, holding deleted files
A company's own logoThat company's specific app (e.g. Word, Chrome)

Why this matters to you

Recognising icons quickly is what lets you navigate a computer without reading every label — a real time-saver once you've used a system for a while, and it's exactly how you'll spot the right app in every course from here on.

🧪 Try it yourself: Look at your desktop or Start Menu and find one folder icon, one shortcut icon (with the small arrow), and one specific app icon. Say how you told them apart.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Icon

A small picture representing a file, folder, or program

Shortcut

An icon with a small arrow, pointing to a file or program kept elsewhere

Study tip: A small arrow in the corner of an icon always means “shortcut” — the real file lives somewhere else.

lessons.title: 2.6 Using the Taskbar
lessons.html:
Using the TaskbarLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
If you have three programs open at once, how do you quickly jump between them without closing anything?

Using the Taskbar

In plain words

The taskbar is the bar, usually at the bottom of the screen, that shows the Start Menu button, open programs, and useful icons like the clock.

Think of the taskbar like a row of open books on a table — each one shows you what's currently “open,” and you can tap any of them to bring it to the front.

What lives on the taskbar

SectionWhat it shows
Start Menu buttonOpens the main menu of programs and settings
Pinned/open programsIcons for programs you've pinned or currently have open
System traySmall icons for things like Wi-Fi, volume, and battery
ClockThe current date and time

Why this matters to you

Instead of closing and reopening a program to switch tasks, clicking its taskbar icon brings it straight back — this alone saves huge amounts of time once you're juggling several windows, which happens constantly in this course.

🧪 Try it yourself: Open two different programs (like a browser and a Notes app). Practice clicking their icons on the taskbar to switch between them without closing either one.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Taskbar

The bar showing open programs, the Start Menu, and the clock

Pin

To keep a program's icon on the taskbar permanently for quick access

System tray

The small group of icons showing things like Wi-Fi and volume

Study tip: The taskbar is your fastest way to switch between open programs — no need to close one to use another.

lessons.title: 2.7 Opening and Closing Programs
lessons.html:
Opening and Closing ProgramsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You've opened an app, used it, and now you're done. What's actually the “right” way to close it?

Opening and Closing Programs

In plain words

Opening a program means starting it up so you can use it. Closing a program means shutting it down properly when you're finished.

Think of opening a program like opening a shop for business, and closing it like locking up properly at the end of the day — you want to make sure everything (your work) is safely put away first.

How to open and close

ActionHow to do it
Open a programDouble-click its icon, or find it in the Start Menu and click once
Close a programClick the X in the top-right corner of its window
Minimise a programClick the — (dash) to hide it without closing
Force-close a stuck programUse Ctrl+Alt+Delete → Task Manager → End Task

Why this matters to you

Closing a program properly gives it a chance to ask “do you want to save your changes?” before anything is lost — clicking X carelessly on unsaved work is one of the most common ways students accidentally lose an assignment.

🧪 Try it yourself: Open a program (like Notepad or a Notes app), type a sentence, then click the X and notice whether it asks you to save. Try saving, then close it again.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Minimise

Hiding a program's window without closing it

Force-close

Shutting down a stuck program using Task Manager

Study tip: Always look for a save prompt before closing — it's the computer's way of protecting your work.

lessons.title: 2.8 Using Windows Search

Using Windows SearchLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You have hundreds of files on a computer. How do you find just ONE of them in seconds instead of scrolling forever?

Using Windows Search

In plain words

Windows Search is a built-in tool that lets you find files, folders, and programs just by typing part of their name.

Think of it like asking a librarian to find a book for you instead of searching every shelf yourself — you just describe what you want, and it's found instantly.

How to search effectively

StepWhat to do
1. Open searchClick the search icon/box next to the Start Menu, or press the Windows key
2. TypeStart typing part of the file, folder, or program name
3. Review resultsLook at the matching files, folders, and apps shown
4. OpenClick the correct result to open it directly

Why this matters to you

Searching is almost always faster than manually clicking through folders, especially once you have many files saved — a skill you'll rely on constantly through the rest of this course.

🧪 Try it yourself: Use Windows Search to find a program you know is installed (like Calculator or Word) by typing just the first few letters of its name.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Search

A tool that finds files, folders, or programs by typing part of their name

Result

A matching file, folder, or program shown after a search

Study tip: You rarely need to remember exactly where a file is saved — just remember part of its name and let Search do the rest.

lessons.title: 3.1 What Is an Operating System?
lessons.html:
What Is an Operating System?Lesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
When you press the power button, something has to be running BEFORE any app can even open. What is that “something”?

What Is an Operating System?

In plain words

An operating system (OS) is the main software that manages all of a computer's hardware and lets you run other programs on top of it.

Think of the operating system as the manager of a busy restaurant: it doesn't cook the food itself, but it makes sure the kitchen, waiters, and dining room all work together smoothly so every other part of the restaurant can function.

What an operating system actually does

JobWhat it means
Manages hardwareControls the screen, keyboard, storage, and memory
Runs programsLets you open and use apps like Word or a browser
Manages filesOrganises everything into files and folders you can find
Provides the interfaceGives you icons, windows, and menus to interact with

Why this matters to you

Every computer, phone, and tablet needs an operating system to function at all — it's the very first thing that loads when you turn a device on, before any app can run.

🧪 Try it yourself: Check what operating system your own phone or computer uses (Settings → About). Is it Windows, macOS, Android, or iOS?

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Operating system (OS)

The main software that manages hardware and runs other programs

Interface

The icons, windows, and menus you use to interact with a computer

Study tip: Every app you'll ever use in this course runs ON TOP of an operating system — it's the foundation everything else is built on.

Introduction to WindowsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
What is “Windows,” exactly — is it the physical glass windows on your house, or something else entirely?

Introduction to Windows

In plain words

Windows is an operating system made by Microsoft, and it's one of the most widely used operating systems on desktop and laptop computers around the world.

If an operating system is a restaurant manager, Windows is one specific, very popular manager — with its own particular style of running things (icons, a Start Menu, a taskbar) that millions of computers around the world use.

What makes Windows recognisable

FeatureWhat it looks like
Start MenuA button (usually bottom-left) opening your programs and settings
TaskbarA bar showing open programs and the clock
File ExplorerThe tool for browsing your files and folders
Windows keyA keyboard key with the Windows logo that opens the Start Menu

Why this matters to you

Much of this Computer Literacy course is taught using Windows because it's the operating system most learners will meet at work, in internet cafés, or at school — knowing it well is a genuinely transferable, employable skill.

Windows

A popular operating system made by Microsoft

Start Menu

The main menu in Windows for opening programs and settings

File Explorer

The Windows tool for browsing files and folders

Study tip: Once you're comfortable with the Start Menu and taskbar, you already understand the two most-used parts of Windows.

Windows DesktopLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Two different Windows computers can have completely different backgrounds and icons, yet still feel instantly familiar to use. Why?

Windows Desktop

In plain words

The Windows Desktop is the main working screen in Windows, shown right after you log in, where your icons, wallpaper, and taskbar all live.

It's familiar across different computers the same way a car's steering wheel and pedals are always roughly in the same place, even in a car you've never driven before.

What you'll always find

ElementPurpose
Desktop iconsQuick access to files, folders, or programs you've placed there
WallpaperThe background picture, which you can personalise
TaskbarShows open programs, the Start Menu, and the clock
Right-click menuA menu of options like “New,” “Sort by,” or “Personalize”

Why this matters to you

Because the layout stays consistent, once you learn one Windows desktop, you can comfortably use almost any other Windows computer — at an internet café, a school lab, or a workplace.

Desktop icon

A shortcut placed directly on the desktop for quick access

Personalize

The Windows option for changing the desktop's look, like the wallpaper

Windows SettingsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You want to change your Wi-Fi network, adjust the screen brightness, or turn on Dark Mode. Where in the world do you even start?

Windows Settings

In plain words

Windows Settings is the central app where you control how your computer looks, behaves, and connects — from Wi-Fi to sound to your account.

Think of Settings like the control panel in a car: one place where every adjustable dial and switch — mirrors, seat position, air conditioning — lives together, instead of being scattered randomly.

Common things you'll adjust

Setting categoryWhat you can change there
SystemDisplay brightness, sound volume, storage
Network & InternetWi-Fi connections, airplane mode
PersonalizationWallpaper, colours, lock screen
AccountsYour user profile, sign-in options
Update & SecuritySoftware updates, antivirus, backups

Instead of guessing or asking someone else every time something needs adjusting, knowing your way around Settings makes you self-sufficient on any Windows computer.

Tap a word to open its definition.

Settings

The central Windows app for adjusting how the computer looks and behaves

The Settings section for changing wallpaper, colours, and appearance

Control Panel

An older Windows tool for managing hardware, programs, and settings

lessons.title: 3.6 Installing Software
lessons.html:
Installing SoftwareLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You want a new app on your computer, but unlike a phone's app store, sometimes you download a file first. What happens after you double-click it?

Installing Software

In plain words

Installing software means adding a new program to your computer so you can open and use it, usually by running a downloaded installer file.

Installing is like assembling furniture: the installer file is the flat-packed box, and running it unpacks and puts all the pieces in the right places so the finished product (the working app) is ready to use.

The typical installation steps

StepWhat happens
1. DownloadYou get the installer file, often ending in .exe
2. Run the installerDouble-click the file to start the process
3. Follow the promptsClick “Next,” accept terms, choose install location
4. FinishThe program appears in your Start Menu, ready to open

Why this matters to you

Always download software from a trusted, official source — an installer from an unfamiliar or suspicious website is one of the most common ways a computer becomes infected with a virus.

🧪 Try it yourself: Think of one program you'd like to install (or already have). Describe, in your own words, the steps you'd follow (or did follow) to install it safely.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Install

To add a new program to a computer so it can be used

Installer

The file you run to begin installing a program

Study tip: Only install software from sources you genuinely trust — an untrustworthy installer can carry a virus along with the app.

lessons.title: 3.7 Uninstalling Software

Uninstalling SoftwareLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A program you installed months ago is now just taking up space and you never use it. How do you properly get rid of it?

Uninstalling Software

In plain words

Uninstalling software means fully removing a program from your computer, freeing up storage space and cleaning up your system.

Uninstalling is like moving out of a rented room properly — you take everything with you, rather than just closing the door and pretending it's empty while your things are still inside.

How to uninstall properly

StepWhat to do
1. Open SettingsGo to Settings → Apps
2. Find the programSearch or scroll to find the app you want to remove
3. UninstallClick the app, then click “Uninstall”
4. ConfirmFollow any final confirmation prompts

Why this matters to you

Just deleting a program's icon from the desktop does NOT actually uninstall it — the program's files stay on your storage, quietly taking up space. Uninstalling properly through Settings removes it completely.

🧪 Try it yourself: Open Settings → Apps and look through the list of installed programs (without uninstalling anything). Notice how much storage space some of them use.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Uninstall

To fully and properly remove a program from a computer

Apps list

The Settings section listing every installed program

Study tip: Deleting a shortcut icon is not the same as uninstalling — always use Settings → Apps to remove a program completely.

Windows UpdatesLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Your computer suddenly restarts on its own overnight and shows “Installing updates, don't turn off your computer.” What was it actually doing?

Windows Updates

In plain words

Windows Updates are improvements Microsoft regularly sends to your computer to fix problems, close security gaps, and add new features.

Think of updates like regular health check-ups: they catch and fix small problems (bugs and security holes) before they become serious, keeping the whole system healthier over time.

Type of updateWhat it does
Security updateCloses gaps that hackers or viruses could use to break in
Bug fixCorrects something that wasn't working correctly
Feature updateAdds new tools or improves existing ones
Driver updateImproves how Windows works with specific hardware

Why this matters to you

Skipping updates for a long time leaves known security gaps open on your computer — this is one of the most common ways computers get infected with viruses, so it's worth allowing updates to install regularly rather than always postponing them.

Copying and Moving Files

In plain words

Copying creates a duplicate of a file in a new location while keeping the original. Moving relocates a file entirely, so it only exists in the new place.

Copying is like photocopying a page — you end up with two identical pages. Moving is like physically carrying the original page to a new folder — there's still only one page, just somewhere else now.

CopyMove
ShortcutCtrl+C then Ctrl+VCtrl+X then Ctrl+V
ResultFile exists in both the old and new locationFile exists only in the new location

Mixing these up is a common mistake — using Copy (Ctrl+C) when you meant Move (Ctrl+X) leaves an unwanted duplicate behind, quietly using up storage space and cluttering your folders.

🤔 Let's start with a question
You send a WhatsApp message and, in less than a second, a friend on another continent receives it. How does a message actually travel that far, that fast?

What Is the Internet?

In plain words

The internet is a giant network connecting billions of computers and devices worldwide, letting them share information with each other.

Think of the internet like a massive postal system for digital information: instead of trucks carrying letters between post offices, cables and signals carry data between connected devices, all over the world.

FactWhat it means
It's a network of networksMillions of smaller networks all connected together
No single ownerNo one company or country owns the whole internet

lessons.title: 5.2 How the Internet Works

How the Internet WorksLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
When you type a website address and press Enter, what actually happens in the few seconds before the page appears?

How the Internet Works

In plain words

The internet works by breaking your request into small data packets, sending them through connected networks to the right destination, and reassembling the response back on your screen.

It's like mailing a large jigsaw puzzle in dozens of small envelopes, each addressed correctly — each piece travels separately, sometimes by a different route, but they all arrive and get reassembled into the full picture at the other end.

The basic journey of a request

StepWhat happens
1. You request a pageYou type an address or click a link
2. Your request travelsIt's broken into packets and sent through your Internet Service Provider
3. It reaches a serverA powerful computer somewhere holds the website's files
4. The server repliesIt sends the page's data back, broken into packets again
5. Your device reassembles itThe browser puts the packets together and shows you the page

Why this matters to you

Understanding this journey explains why a slow or unstable connection makes pages “buffer” or load partially — some packets are simply taking longer to arrive or get lost along the way and need to be resent.

🧪 Try it yourself: Next time a webpage loads slowly, notice how images or text sometimes appear gradually rather than all at once — that's packets arriving over time.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Server

A powerful computer that stores and sends website files when requested

Internet Service Provider (ISP)

The company that connects your home or device to the internet

Study tip: A webpage loading is really thousands of small pieces of data arriving and being reassembled in front of you — it just happens fast enough to look instant.

In plain words

A search engine is a website (like Google) that helps you find other websites and information by typing in keywords.

A search engine is like an enormous, instant index for the entire internet — you describe roughly what you want, and it hands you a ranked list of the best matches.

Popular search engines

Search engineNotes
GoogleThe most widely used search engine worldwide
BingMicrosoft's search engine, built into Edge
YahooAn older, still-active search engine

Why this matters to you

Search engines are the doorway to nearly all information on the internet — from research for school, to finding a business, to simply answering a curious question, this skill supports almost everything else in this course.

🧪 Try it yourself: Use a search engine to look up the answer to a genuine question you're curious about today, and notice how the results are ranked.

A website that helps you find information and other websites

Keyword

A word or short phrase you type into a search engine to describe what you want

Searching with quotation marks to find an exact matching phrase

You have six different websites open at once for a school project. How do you keep track of all of them without getting lost?

Opening and Managing Web Pages

In plain words

Managing web pages means organising the multiple tabs and windows you have open so you can navigate between them without confusion.

Managing tabs is like keeping several books open on a desk with your finger holding each page — the more you have open, the more important it is to know exactly where each one is.

Downloading Files From the InternetLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You click a link that says “Download,” and a file appears somewhere on your computer moments later. But where exactly did it go?

Downloading Files From the Internet

In plain words

Downloading means copying a file from the internet onto your own device so you can use it even without an internet connection.

Downloading is like borrowing a book from an online library and bringing your own physical copy home — once it's downloaded, it's genuinely yours to open anytime.

StepWhat happens
1. Click DownloadYou select a file you want to save
2. The file transfersYour browser copies the file from the internet to your device
3. It's savedUsually in a “Downloads” folder, unless you chose otherwise
4. You can open itFind it in Downloads and open it like any other file

lessons.title: 6.1 Internet Safety Basics
lessons.html:
Internet Safety BasicsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You'd probably lock your front door before leaving home. Do you take similar basic precautions before using the internet?

Internet Safety Basics

In plain words

Internet safety means the everyday habits that protect you and your information from scams, viruses, and strangers online.

Think of internet safety like road safety: a few simple, consistent habits (looking both ways, wearing a seatbelt) prevent the vast majority of accidents — online safety works the same way.

Core safety habits

HabitWhy it matters
Use strong, unique passwordsMakes it harder for someone to break into your accounts
Think before you clickUnfamiliar links are a common trap
Don't share personal details publiclyProtects you from scams and identity theft
Keep software updatedCloses known security gaps
Trust your instinctsIf something feels wrong or too good to be true, it usually is

Why this matters to you

These simple habits are your everyday shield online — most successful scams and hacks don't rely on advanced tricks, they rely on someone skipping one of these basic precautions.

🧪 Try it yourself: Look at your own most-used online account (email or social media). Check: do you have a strong password on it? When did you last change it?

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Internet safety

Everyday habits that protect you online

Personal information

Study tip: Most online safety comes down to a handful of simple, repeated habits — not complicated technical tricks.

Creating Strong PasswordsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Is “password123” actually a safe password? How long do you think it would take someone (or a computer) to guess it?

Creating Strong Passwords

In plain words

A strong password is one that's long, unpredictable, and unique to each account, making it very hard for someone else to guess or crack.

A weak password is like a flimsy padlock anyone could snap open; a strong password is like a heavy-duty lock that would take far too long and effort to break through.

What makes a password strong

RuleExample
At least 12 characters longLonger is always harder to crack
Mix letters, numbers, and symbolsTr0piC@lRain!2026
Avoid obvious personal infoNot your name, birthday, or “password”
Use a different password per accountSo one leak doesn't expose everything

Why this matters to you

A weak, reused password is one of the single biggest reasons accounts get hacked — strengthening this one habit protects your email, social media, and even your money in online banking.

🧪 Try it yourself: Test one of your current passwords against the rules in the table above. If it's weak, write down (privately) a stronger replacement using the same rules.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Strong password

A long, unpredictable password that's hard to guess or crack

Password manager

A tool that securely stores and remembers strong passwords for you

Study tip: A long, unique password for every important account is one of the cheapest, most effective security upgrades you can make today.

lessons.title: 6.3 Two-Factor Authentication

Two-Factor AuthenticationLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Even with a strong password, what if someone still somehow guesses or steals it? Is there a backup layer of protection?

Two-Factor Authentication

In plain words

Two-factor authentication (2FA) is an extra security step that requires a second proof of identity — like a code sent to your phone — in addition to your password.

Think of it like a bank vault needing both a key AND a combination code — even if someone gets hold of one, they still can't get in without the other.

How 2FA typically works

StepWhat happens
1. You enter your passwordThe first proof of identity
2. A code is sent to youUsually via SMS, email, or an authenticator app
3. You enter that codeThe second proof of identity
4. You're logged inOnly after BOTH steps succeed

Why this matters to you

Turning on 2FA for your email and social media means that even if a scammer somehow learns your password, they still can't get into your account without also having your phone — a huge extra layer of protection.

🧪 Try it yourself: Check whether your email account has two-factor authentication available in its security settings, and consider turning it on if you haven't already.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Two-factor authentication (2FA)

A security step requiring a second proof of identity beyond your password

Authenticator app

An app that generates secure codes used for two-factor authentication

Study tip: Turning on two-factor authentication takes a few minutes but makes your accounts dramatically harder to break into.

lessons.title: 6.4 Recognizing Phishing Scams
lessons.html:
Recognizing Phishing ScamsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You get an email saying “Your bank account will be closed — click here immediately to verify your details!” Is this real?

Recognizing Phishing Scams

In plain words

Phishing is a scam where someone pretends to be a trustworthy person or company to trick you into giving away personal information, like passwords or bank details.

Phishing is like someone in a fake uniform knocking on your door claiming to be from the electric company just to get inside your house — the disguise is convincing, but the intent is dishonest.

Warning signs of phishing

Warning signWhy it's suspicious
Urgent, scary language“Act now or lose your account!” pressures you to skip thinking carefully
Misspelled or unusual sender addressReal companies rarely send from odd, misspelled emails
Asking for passwords or codesLegitimate companies almost never ask this by email
Suspicious linksThe link text doesn't match where it actually leads

Why this matters to you

Recognising these signs protects you from losing money, having accounts stolen, or having your identity used by someone else — phishing is one of the most common scams precisely because it looks so convincing at first glance.

🧪 Try it yourself: Think of (or find, without clicking anything) an example of a suspicious message you've received. Identify at least two phishing warning signs in it.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Phishing

A scam that impersonates a trustworthy source to steal your information

Sender address

The actual email address a message came from, which can reveal a fake

Study tip: When a message pressures you to act immediately or share sensitive details, slow down — that pressure is itself a warning sign.

Avoiding Online ScamsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
“Congratulations! You've won $10,000! Click here to claim your prize!” — have you ever seen a message like this? What should you do about it?

Avoiding Online Scams

In plain words

Online scams are dishonest schemes designed to trick you out of money, information, or access to your accounts, often by promising something too good to be true.

Scammers rely on excitement or fear to stop you from thinking clearly — a genuine prize, refund, or emergency almost never requires you to act within minutes or pay a fee upfront to “release” it.

Common scam types

Scam typeHow it works
Prize/lottery scamClaims you've won something you never entered
Fake tech supportClaims your device has a virus and demands payment to “fix” it
Romance scamBuilds a fake online relationship, then asks for money
Job offer scamOffers a job requiring an upfront payment or personal banking details

Why this matters to you

Being able to recognise these patterns protects your money and your peace of mind — scams cost real people real losses every single day, and the patterns rarely change even as the specific stories do.

Scam

A dishonest scheme designed to trick you out of money or information

Too good to be true

A common warning sign that an offer is likely a scam

Protecting Personal Information OnlineLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Would you hand a stranger on the street your home address, phone number, and school name all at once? So why post it all publicly online?

Protecting Personal Information Online

In plain words

Protecting personal information means being careful about what private details — your address, ID number, phone number, passwords — you share online and with whom.

Personal information online is like cash in your wallet: you don't hand it to just anyone who asks, and you keep track of exactly who you've given it to and why.

What to protect and how

Information typeHow to protect it
PasswordsNever share them, even with someone claiming to be “support”
Home address/phone numberOnly share with trusted, verified contacts
ID/financial detailsOnly enter on official, secure (https) websites
LocationTurn off unnecessary location sharing on apps

Why this matters to you

Once personal information is posted publicly or given to the wrong person, it can be used for scams, identity theft, or even physical safety risks — protecting it is far easier than undoing the damage afterward.

Tap a word to open its definition.

Personal information

Private details like your address, ID number, or passwords

Privacy settings

The controls on an account that decide who can see your information

lessons.title: 6.7 Safe Downloads

Safe DownloadsLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A pop-up suddenly claims “Your computer is infected! Download this program NOW to fix it!” Should you click download?

Safe Downloads

In plain words

Safe downloading means only downloading files and programs from trusted, official sources, to avoid accidentally installing viruses or scams.

Think of downloading like eating food from a stranger versus a trusted restaurant — the “free” option from an unverified source can carry hidden risks you can't see just by looking at it.

How to download safely

RuleWhy it matters
Only use official app stores or the software's real websiteReduces the risk of a disguised virus

Scan downloaded files if unsureAntivirus software can check a file before you open it

Following these simple habits is one of the most effective ways to prevent viruses and malware from ever reaching your computer in the first place — prevention is far easier than fixing an infected device afterward.

Computer Viruses and MalwareLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Your computer suddenly runs very slowly, shows strange pop-up ads, or files start disappearing. What could be causing this?

Computer Viruses and Malware

In plain words

Malware (short for “malicious software”) is any harmful software designed to damage, steal from, or take control of your computer. A virus is one common type of malware.

Malware is like a harmful germ getting into a body — it sneaks in (often through an unsafe download or link), then spreads and causes damage from the inside.

Common types of malware

TypeWhat it does
VirusAttaches to files and spreads, damaging or corrupting them
RansomwareLocks your files and demands payment to unlock them
SpywareSecretly watches what you do and steals information
AdwareFloods your screen with unwanted advertisements

Why this matters to you

Recognising the warning signs of malware — sudden slowness, strange pop-ups, unfamiliar programs — helps you catch an infection early and get help before serious damage or data loss occurs.

🧪 Try it yourself: List any warning signs from the table above that you've personally noticed on a device before. If none, describe what you'd do if you noticed one tomorrow.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Malware

Any harmful software designed to damage or exploit a computer

Virus

A type of malware that attaches to files and spreads

Antivirus software

A program that detects and removes malware

Study tip: Slow performance and strange pop-ups are your computer's way of telling you something may be wrong — don't ignore them.

lessons.title: 7.1 What Is Email?

What Is Email?Lesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Before phones could text, how do you think people sent written messages instantly over the internet? The answer still matters today.

What Is Email?

In plain words

Email (electronic mail) is a way of sending written messages, and often files, over the internet from one account to another, almost instantly.

🤔 Let's start with a question
You've spent an hour writing an important document. The power suddenly goes out. Is your work gone forever?

Saving a Word Document

In plain words

Saving a document means storing your work permanently on your computer or in the cloud, so it survives even after you close Word or lose power.

Saving is like writing your homework in ink in a notebook, instead of on a whiteboard that gets wiped clean the moment the lights go out — it makes your work permanent, not temporary.

Save (Ctrl+S)

To store your document permanently so it survives closing the program

Save As

To save a copy of a document under a new name or location

Data

🤔 Let's start with a question

Basic Excel Formulas

In plain words

A formula in Excel is an instruction, starting with an equals sign (=), that tells Excel to calculate something automatically, like a sum or an average.

A formula is like giving Excel a recipe instead of doing the cooking yourself — you tell it what to combine and how, and it produces the result instantly, every time the ingredients change.

FormulaWhat it doesExample

=A1*A2Multiplies two cells5 * 3 = 15
=A1/A2Divides one cell by another6 / 3 = 2

Why this matters to you

The real power of a formula is that if you change the original numbers, the result updates automatically — you never have to recalculate by hand, even if you change the numbers a hundred times.

Formula

In plain words

Sorting rearranges the rows in a spreadsheet based on a chosen column — like putting numbers smallest-to-largest, or names A-to-Z.

Sorting is like shuffling a stack of exam papers into order by score before handing them back — nothing about the actual scores changes, only the order they're arranged in.

How to sort data

StepWhat to do
1. Select your dataClick and drag to highlight the range you want to sort
2. Go to Data tabClick “Sort”
3. Choose the columnPick which column to sort by (e.g. “Score”)
4. Choose orderAscending (A–Z, smallest-to-largest) or Descending (Z–A, largest-to-smallest)

Why this matters to you

Sorting instantly reveals patterns — the top performer, the lowest expense, the earliest date — that would otherwise take ages to spot by scanning an unsorted list manually.

🧪 Try it yourself: Enter five students' names and random scores into two columns, select the data, and sort it so the highest score appears first.

Sort

Rearranging rows based on the values in a chosen column

Ascending/Descending

Sorting smallest-to-largest, or largest-to-smallest

You have 200 rows of sales data, but only want to see entries from March. Do you have to scroll through all 200 rows yourself?

Filtering Data

In plain words

Filtering temporarily hides rows that don't match a condition you choose, showing only the specific data you want to focus on.

Filtering is like using a sieve to separate out just the ingredients you need from a big mixed bowl — everything else is still there, just temporarily out of view.

How filtering works

StepWhat to do
1. Select your dataHighlight the range including your column headers
2. Go to Data tabClick “Filter”
3. Click the dropdown arrowAppears next to each column header
4. Choose what to showTick only the values you want visible

Filtering lets you focus instantly on exactly the information you need — like only March's sales, or only students who scored below 50% — without deleting or losing any of the other data.

Filter

A tool that temporarily hides rows that don't match a chosen condition

This project asks you to bring together everything from this module — entering data, formulas, functions, formatting, sorting, filtering, and a chart — into one complete, working spreadsheet.

In plain words

Microsoft PowerPoint is a program used to create slide-based presentations, combining text, images, and design to support a spoken presentation.

Think of PowerPoint as a set of large, visual flashcards you flip through while speaking — each slide highlights one key idea, keeping your audience focused and engaged.

UseExample
School presentationsA class project or book report
Business pitchesProposing an idea to investors or a boss

The PowerPoint interface is the layout of tools and panels you see when creating a presentation — the slide area, the slide list, and the Ribbon of tools.

lessons.title: 10.3 Creating a Presentation

Creating a PresentationLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You've opened PowerPoint. There's one blank slide. How do you actually start building a full, multi-slide presentation from here?

Creating a Presentation

In plain words

Creating a presentation means starting a new PowerPoint file and building it out, slide by slide, around your topic.

Building a presentation is like planning a short spoken story — you need a clear beginning (introduction), a middle (main points), and an end (conclusion), with one slide dedicated to each key idea.

Steps to start a presentation

StepWhat to do
1. Open PowerPointChoose “Blank Presentation” or a template
2. Add a title slideType your topic and, optionally, your name
3. Add new slidesClick “New Slide” for each additional point
4. Save itGive it a clear file name

Why this matters to you

Planning your key points BEFORE opening PowerPoint (even just a short list) makes the whole building process faster and produces a clearer, more focused final presentation.

🧪 Try it yourself: Create a new presentation with a title slide about any topic you like, then add two more slides, each with a different simple point.

Tap a word to open its definition.

Title slide

The first slide, usually showing the presentation's topic and presenter

New Slide

The button used to add another slide to your presentation

In plain words

Adding and editing slides means inserting new slides wherever needed, and changing, reordering, or deleting existing ones.

Editing your slide order is like rearranging pages in a photo album — you can insert a new page anywhere, remove one you don't need, or move pages around until the story flows correctly.

ActionHow to do it
Add a slideRight-click in the slide panel → New Slide
Delete a slideRight-click the slide in the panel → Delete Slide
Reorder slidesClick and drag a slide up or down in the panel

Being comfortable rearranging slides means you never have to rebuild a presentation from scratch just because you realise a better order partway through — you can simply drag things into place.

Adding Text and Images

In plain words

Adding text and images means filling your slides with the words and pictures that carry your actual message to the audience.

Well-chosen text and images make a slide instantly clearer and more memorable — but cramming too much text onto one slide is one of the most common presentation mistakes, since your audience ends up reading instead of listening to you.

A box on a slide where you can type words

A consistent, well-chosen theme makes your presentation look far more professional and put-together with almost no extra effort — a single click can transform a plain presentation instantly.

Theme

When you click to move from one slide to the next, does it just jump instantly, or can it change smoothly?

A slide transition is a visual effect that plays as you move from one slide to the next, like a fade or a slide-in motion.

🧪 Try it yourself: Apply a simple, subtle transition (like “Fade”) to one slide in your test presentation, and preview how it looks.

Transition

A visual effect that plays when moving between two slides

The Ribbon tab where you choose and apply transition effects

Your laptop is stolen or your phone breaks. Are your important files gone forever, or is there a safer place to keep them?

StepWhat to do

Copying a file from your device up into Google Drive

Sharing Files and FoldersLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You and a classmate need to work on the exact same document together. Do you have to email a new copy back and forth every time either of you makes a change?

Sharing Files and Folders

In plain words

Sharing a file or folder in Google Drive gives another person access to view or edit it directly, without sending separate copies back and forth.

Sharing is like handing someone a key to the same locked room, rather than photocopying everything inside it for them separately — you're both looking at, and can both edit, the exact same original.

How to share

StepWhat to do
1. Right-click the file/folderChoose “Share”
2. Enter their emailType the person's Google account email
3. Choose their permission“Viewer,” “Commenter,” or “Editor”
4. Click SendThey receive access, often with an email notification

Why this matters to you

Sharing removes the confusion and wasted time of emailing multiple versions of the same file back and forth — everyone works from a single, always-current version instead.

Share

Giving another person access to view or edit a file or folder

Permission level

How much access someone has: Viewer, Commenter, or Editor

Google Docs is Google's free, browser-based word processor — similar to Microsoft Word — that saves automatically and lets multiple people edit the same document at once.

A friend sends you a link and says “join my meeting at 3pm.” What do you actually do with that link?

StepWhat to do

Backing up means keeping an extra copy of your important files in a second location — like Google Drive or a USB drive — so you don't lose everything if one device fails.

In plain words

Troubleshooting is the step-by-step process of identifying and fixing a computer problem yourself, starting with the simplest possible causes first.

StepWhat to check

lessons.title: 14.3 Creating a Professional Presentation
lessons.html:
Creating a Professional PresentationLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You know how to add slides, themes, and animations in PowerPoint. But what separates a presentation that looks amateur from one that looks genuinely polished?

Creating a Professional Presentation

In plain words

A professional presentation combines a clear structure, consistent design, and appropriate use of text, images, and effects to communicate confidently to a real audience.

A professional presentation is like a well-rehearsed performance — every part (slides, visuals, delivery) works together smoothly, instead of feeling rushed, cluttered, or inconsistent.

What makes a presentation professional

ElementWhy it matters
One consistent themeNot mixing several unrelated themes or colour schemes
Short, clear bullet pointsNot paragraphs of text crammed onto one slide
Purposeful imagesRelevant visuals, not random decoration
Minimal, tasteful transitions/animationsSupport the message, don't distract from it

Why this matters to you

A clean, well-designed, and well-rehearsed presentation can make the difference between an audience genuinely engaging with your message and simply tuning out — a real, practical skill for school and work alike.

🧪 Try it yourself: Take the practice presentation you built earlier in this course and review it against the table above, adjusting anything that feels cluttered or inconsistent.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Professional presentation

A clear, consistently designed presentation that communicates effectively

Cluttered slide

A slide with too much text, too many images, or inconsistent design

Study tip: If a slide feels crowded, that's usually a sign to split it into two simpler slides instead of shrinking the text to fit.

questions.question: Why should slides use large, readable fonts?

lessons.title: 14.4 Professional Email Communication
lessons.html:
Professional Email CommunicationLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
You already know how to send an email and its basic etiquette. But how do you write one specifically for a job application, a boss, or an official organisation?

Professional Email Communication

In plain words

Professional email communication means applying email etiquette specifically to formal, workplace, or official situations — where tone and clarity matter even more.

A professional email is like a formal letter delivered instantly — it still needs the same respectful structure and careful wording, just adapted to email's faster, more direct format.

A professional email checklist

ElementExample
Clear, specific subject line“Application for Computer Literacy Instructor Role” not “Hi”
Formal greeting“Dear Mrs. Johnson,” rather than “Hey”
Concise, well-organised bodyState your purpose clearly in the first sentence or two
Professional sign-off“Sincerely,” or “Best regards,” followed by your full name
Proofread before sendingNo typos, especially in a job application or official request

Why this matters to you

A well-written professional email can be the deciding factor in whether an employer, school, or organisation responds to you positively — it's often your very first impression before anyone meets you in person.

🧪 Try it yourself: Write a practice professional email — for example, applying for an opportunity or requesting information from an organisation — following every item in the checklist above.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Professional tone

Formal, respectful, and clear language suited to a workplace or official context

Sign-off

The formal closing phrase and name at the end of a professional email

Study tip: State your purpose in the very first sentence — a busy recipient should understand what you need without having to read your whole email first.

lessons.title: 14.5 Managing Digital Files
lessons.html:
Managing Digital FilesLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
At work, you might handle hundreds of files across email, Drive, and your own computer. How do you keep all of that under control long-term?

Managing Digital Files

In plain words

Managing digital files at a professional level means applying everything from earlier in this course — organising, naming, backing up — consistently, across every place you keep files.

Think of this as running your own small “filing department” — one where naming, storing, and backing up files properly is treated as a genuine ongoing responsibility, not an occasional afterthought.

Professional file management habits

HabitWhy it matters
Consistent naming conventions“2026-Report-January.docx” is easier to sort than “Doc1.docx”
One clear folder structureApplied consistently across your computer and cloud storage
Regular backupsImportant work files should never exist in only one place
Periodic clean-upRemoving outdated or duplicate files regularly

Why this matters to you

Employers and organisations rely on people who can manage shared files responsibly — being known as someone whose files are always easy to find and well-organised is a genuinely valuable professional reputation.

🧪 Try it yourself: Choose a consistent file naming pattern (like “Year-Topic-Name”) and rename three of your own existing files to follow it.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Naming convention

A consistent pattern used to name files so they sort and search well

Folder structure

The overall, consistent way folders and subfolders are organised

Study tip: A consistent naming pattern (like starting with the year) makes files sort in a sensible order automatically, without any extra effort.

lessons.title: 14.6 Online Collaboration
lessons.html:
Online CollaborationLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
A modern workplace often has people working from different locations, sometimes different countries. How do teams like that actually get anything done together?

Online Collaboration

In plain words

Online collaboration means working together with others digitally — through shared documents, video calls, and messaging — even when you're not in the same physical place.

Online collaboration combines nearly everything from this course: Google Docs/Sheets/Slides for shared work, Google Meet or Zoom for discussion, and email for formal communication — all working together.

Core online collaboration skills

Skill (from earlier in this course)Role in collaboration
Sharing files/folders (Module 11)Gives teammates access to the same documents
Google Docs/Sheets/Slides (Module 11)Lets multiple people edit the same file together, live
Video calls (Module 12)Supports real-time discussion and decision-making
Professional email (this module)Handles formal updates and requests

Why this matters to you

Being comfortable combining these tools smoothly is exactly what real remote and hybrid workplaces expect today — this single ability can make you significantly more employable in a modern job market.

🧪 Try it yourself: Think through a hypothetical group project: which tool from the table would you use for sharing the plan, which for discussing it live, and which for the final formal update? Explain your choices.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Collaboration

Working together with others to accomplish a shared goal

Remote work

Working from a different location than your teammates, often digitally connected

Study tip: Different tasks call for different tools — live discussion works best by video call, while shared ongoing work works best in a shared document.

lessons.title: 14.7 Digital Workplace Safety
lessons.html:
Digital Workplace SafetyLesson note
🤔 Let's start with a question
Everything you've learned about online safety earlier in this course — does it still apply once you're using a computer specifically for work?

Digital Workplace Safety

In plain words

Digital workplace safety applies the internet safety and security habits from earlier in this course specifically to a work environment, where the stakes (company data, client information) can be even higher.

Think of workplace safety like wearing safety gear on a construction site — many of the same general safety habits apply everywhere, but a workplace often has extra rules because more is at stake if something goes wrong.

Key digital workplace safety habits

HabitWhy it matters at work
Never share your work passwordProtects not just you, but company or client data
Be extra cautious with work email attachments/linksBusinesses are common phishing targets
Keep work and personal accounts separateReduces risk and confusion
Report suspicious activity immediatelyA quick report can prevent a larger security incident
Lock your screen when stepping awayPrevents anyone else from accessing your open work

Why this matters to you

A single careless click on a phishing email or a shared password can affect an entire organisation, not just one person — this is why professional workplaces take digital safety especially seriously.

🧪 Try it yourself: Think about your own current habits (even outside a formal workplace): do you lock your screen when stepping away? Would you recognise a phishing email if it appeared in a work inbox?

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Workplace safety

Applying strong digital security habits specifically in a work context

Security incident

An event where data, accounts, or systems may have been compromised

Study tip: Locking your screen every single time you step away, even briefly, is a small habit that meaningfully protects both you and your workplace.

questions.question: What is a safe habit when you step away from your work computer?
options: Leave it fully open and logged in
Lock the screen so others cannot use it
questions.explanation: Locking the screen protects your work and data while you are away.
